read: partial: pp. 1-9 (abstract, 1 introduction, 2 related work, 3 benchmark construction, 4 evaluation, 5 conclusion, limitations) in full; appendices A-E (pp. 12-13) read; appendix F result tables (pp. 14-16) skimmed
venue_now: The text is arXiv 2412.06559v4, 26 May 2025, dated 2025-05-27 (p. 1), with no venue line. Other papers in this corpus cite it as ACL 2025 (Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting, Volume 1, pp. 1009-1024).
what_it_is: ProcessBench measures the ability to identify the earliest erroneous step in math solutions (abstract, p. 1). Problems come from the test sets of GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH; solutions come from twelve open Qwen and LLaMA models, re-segmented into paragraphs by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and balanced between correct and incorrect final answers (pp. 4-5). Doctoral-level math experts, given the reference solutions, label the earliest error or 'all correct'; each solution goes to three experts and up to five until three agree, and about 30% are discarded (pp. 4-5). The 3,400 cases (Table 2, p. 5) are used to evaluate PRMs and prompted critic LLMs by the F1 of their accuracies on erroneous and on correct samples (p. 6).
domain: math, grade-school to Olympiad level (GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH)
size: 3,400 test cases: 400 GSM8K and 1,000 each for MATH, OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH (Table 2, p. 5; Table 4, p. 12); solutions from 12 open models (p. 4); 6 PRMs and 19 prompted critic models evaluated (Table 3, p. 7; my count)
source_of_items: existing grade-school and competition math datasets (test sets); solutions generated by open LLMs; error labels by human experts
has_gold_traces: partial: expert labels of the earliest erroneous step per solution (pp. 3-5); the source datasets' reference solutions were shown to annotators (p. 5) but play no part in scoring
evaluation: step-level: locate the earliest erroneous step or declare all steps correct; F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples (pp. 3-4, 6)
human_validation: Annotators have doctoral-level mathematical expertise and passed a proficiency examination and tutorial (p. 4). Three experts per solution, extended to five until three agree; solutions without agreement (about 30%) are discarded, as are rare cases where a wrong final answer was labelled all-correct (p. 5). The share of cases settled by 3-of-3 agreement ranges from 47.8% (Omni-MATH, wrong answers) to 95.9% (GSM8K, correct answers) (Table 2, p. 5). The limitations allow that labels may still be inaccurate on Olympiad-level problems and that discarding may bias the distribution (p. 9).
contamination_measures: none for the benchmark (public test sets, p. 4); for the authors' own PRM, PRM800K training samples sharing problems with ProcessBench were removed (p. 13)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper. Belongs in the process supervision and judge validity paragraph as the reference benchmark for step-error identification; NEXT_CYCLE_REVIEW sec. 4.2 names it (brief sec. 6). Two findings bear directly on EngTrace: existing PRMs underperform prompted critic models and degrade on harder problems (p. 1; p. 8), and the share of correct-answer solutions containing a process error grows with difficulty, from 3.5% on GSM8K to 51.8% on Omni-MATH (Table 2, p. 5; p. 6), the math counterpart of EngTrace's correct-answer traces with incorrect steps (93 of 228; brief sec. 3).

suggested_wording: ProcessBench (Zheng et al., 2025) asks PRMs and prompted critic models to locate the earliest erroneous step in 3,400 expert-labelled solutions to grade-school to Olympiad math problems, and finds that existing PRMs trail prompted critics and that correct final answers hide process errors more often as problems get harder (3.5% of correct-answer solutions on GSM8K, 51.8% on Omni-MATH).
facts_to_cite: 3,400 test cases from the GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH test sets; the task is to identify the earliest erroneous step or conclude that all steps are correct (abstract, p. 1; pp. 3-4).

Solutions are generated by twelve open Qwen and LLaMA models and labelled by doctoral-level math experts, three per solution and up to five until three agree; about 30% are discarded for lack of agreement (pp. 4-5).
Among solutions with correct final answers, the share containing a process error is 3.5% (GSM8K), 18.8% (MATH), 32.2% (OlympiadBench) and 51.8% (Omni-MATH) (Table 2, p. 5; p. 6).

Existing PRMs fail to generalise beyond GSM8K and MATH and underperform prompted critic models: average F1 31.5 for Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and 56.5 for the authors' PRM800K-trained Qwen2.5-Math-7B, against 61.9 for GPT-4o, 71.5 for QwQ-32B-Preview and 87.9 for o1-mini (abstract, p. 1; Table 3, p. 7; p. 8).
The F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples, chosen to balance over-criticism against missed errors (p. 6).
The authors attribute the PRMs' weakness to Monte Carlo step labels, which depend on the generating model and are invalidated when correct answers follow erroneous steps (pp. 8-9).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares step-level error identification on quantitative derivations, expert human labels (doctoral-level math, p. 4), and the comparison of PRMs with prompted LLM critics that EngTrace makes with the Qwen PRMs and its judges (brief sec. 3). Lacks: generated instances (static public test sets, p. 4); gold intermediate values (labels are first-error positions on model outputs; references were only shown to annotators, p. 5); labels after the first error (EngTrace's experts label every step, PILOT_SUMMARY sec. 1.3); engineering (math only); an agreement coefficient (it reports how many annotators were needed to reach three agreeing, Table 2, p. 5, after discarding about 30%). ProcessBench evaluates verifiers only; EngTrace validates evaluators against experts and also scores the solving models.
notes: Model-name caution: ProcessBench's 'Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K' (Appendix C, p. 13) is not the Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B that EngTrace ran; the 72B's ProcessBench F1 of 78.3 is reported by the Qwen lessons paper (zhang2025prmlessons Table 7, p. 10), not by ProcessBench. For the Skywork PRMs the step threshold was chosen on the GSM8K subset (p. 7). ProcessBench's error definition explicitly covers incorrect calculations as well as logical, conceptual and completeness errors (p. 4), so its process-error rates are closer to EngTrace's step labels than Uesato's major-mistake criterion, but annotators, domains and step segmentation differ, so the rates are not directly comparable.
